name: Gelatin filler

lead: Gelatin is one of the naturally derived polymers listed among materials used in injectable dermal fillers, together with hyaluronic acid, collagen and chitosan. Fillers are injected to add volume or smooth lines in the face.
Gelatin is made by partially breaking down collagen, and collagen-based fillers were the first to be FDA-approved, in 1981. Their effects are reported to last about three to four months.

paras: Dermal fillers are injected by clinicians into the skin or deeper facial tissue. Some are resorbable and others are not.
General filler risks include bruising, redness, pain, infection, allergic reactions, lumps, and rarely vascular events that can cause skin necrosis or blindness.

angle.text: Like other fillers, it is used by clinicians to fill and contour areas of the face and soften lines. Gelatin-based hydrogels are a resorbable material type, so the result is temporary.

lead: Gelatin is a protein made by partially breaking down collagen from animal skin and bones, and it appears in the dermal-filler literature as a naturally derived polymer for injectable fillers, alongside hyaluronic acid, collagen and chitosan.[1][2] Someone choosing a filler of this kind is looking to add volume under the skin or soften lines, giving a fuller, smoother-looking area of the face.[1]

Gelatin sits close to the collagen fillers that started the modern filler era. Bovine collagen products Zyderm and Zyplast were the first fillers offered to US dermatologists in the early 1980s, with skin testing typically required beforehand.[3] Wikipedia's gelatin article describes collagen dermal fillers as FDA-approved and as lasting about three to four months.[2]
Gelatin-specific cosmetic fillers have little published literature of their own, so most of what is documented concerns fillers as a class and the collagen products from which gelatin derives.

paras: Natural polymers used in dermal fillers include gelatin, collagen, hyaluronic acid and chitosan; synthetic options include polyethylene glycol and poly(lactic acid).[1] Fillers may be resorbable or non-resorbable and are often prepared as hydrogels; they became widely used in the 1980s, and collagen-type fillers have used glutaraldehyde cross-linking to improve integration with tissue.[1]

Gelatin is produced from by-products of the meat and leather industries such as pork skin, cattle bones and hides, through pretreatment, hydrolysis, extraction and refining. It dissolves in hot water and forms a gel on cooling, holding up to 90 percent water.[2] Gelatin hydrogels are described as biodegradable and biocompatible and are used in tissue engineering and drug delivery as well as in fillers.[2]

Bovine collagen (Zyderm) became the first FDA-approved filler in 1981; it needed allergy testing beforehand and typically lasted a few months.[4] Hyaluronic acid fillers such as Restylane and Juvederm followed from the late 1990s, with a lower risk of allergic reaction and durations of roughly six to twelve months.[4] The first injectable hyaluronic acid filler was described in 1989.[3]
Later products such as Artecoll and ArteFill pair PMMA microspheres with a rapidly dissolving bovine collagen carrier; ArteFill received FDA approval in October 2006.[3]

General filler risks include bruising, redness, pain or itching, infection, and allergic reactions causing lumps or scarring. Vascular events can occur: retrograde embolization can cause permanent blindness, and delayed skin necrosis has been reported.[1]

Gelatin allergy affects a small portion of the population, and in injected vaccines it has caused severe systemic reactions, which led some countries to phase it out of vaccines.[2] For animal-derived collagen fillers, skin testing was routine in the early products.[3] Gelatin is also a point of dietary and religious consideration: halal, kosher, Buddhist, Hindu and Jain practices have differing positions on animal-derived gelatin.[2]

timeline.event: Bovine collagen filler Zyderm becomes the first FDA-approved dermal filler.[4]
First injectable hyaluronic acid filler described.[3]
ArteFill (PMMA microspheres in a collagen carrier) receives FDA approval.[3]
